turns.reply: Welcome, I'm glad you're here! Think of a hot mug of tea left on your desk: what happens to it over the next hour?

Yes, it cools down, and it cools fastest at first. A radioactive sample does something similar: its radioactivity fades over time, and the time it takes to fall to half is called its half-life.

If a sample's radioactivity starts at 800 and one half-life passes, what will it have fallen to?

That's fine, let's make it simpler. To halve something just means to cut it in half, like splitting a chocolate bar between two people so each gets half.

If you halve 800, what number do you get?

Yes, 400 is right: half of 800. So after one half-life, 800 falls to 400, and after a second half-life it halves again.

After two half-lives, what would the radioactivity have fallen to?

Yes, 200 is right: half of 400. The number of decays each second is called activity, measured in becquerels (Bq), where 1 Bq means 1 decay per second.

If a sample has an activity of 50 Bq, how many decays happen every second?

Yes, 50 decays a second is right, because 1 Bq means 1 decay per second. The count rate is the number of decays a detector actually records each second, like a clicker counting what it picks up.

If a sample's activity falls from 50 Bq to half, what activity is that?

Count rate is how many decays a detector actually picks up each second, like a clicker counting clicks. Activity is how many decays really happen each second.

Say a detector records 30 decays in one second. If we wait one half-life, what would the count rate fall to?

Yes, 15 is right: half of 30, because one half-life halves the count rate. That means a detector counting 30 decays a second drops to 15 after one half-life.

If we wait one more half-life, what would the count rate fall to?

turns.reply: Yes, a break is fine, and you can come back to this lesson any time. The count rate works a bit like that, as it keeps dropping every half-life. If we wait one more half-life, what would the count rate fall to?
This bit is a tricky one, so no worries. Do you want me to just tell you the rest of this one?

Fair enough, here's the rest. Her answer of 5 was off: it's 15 halved, so 7.5, and after 2 half-lives it's 1/4 of the start, a net decline of 3/4. Radioactive decay is random, so you can't predict one nucleus, but with huge numbers the overall rate is predictable. After n half-lives, activity = A₀ × (½)ⁿ, and a decay graph never reaches zero. Look at the diagram: the activity halves every 2 hours, so the half-life is 2 hours.

Next, a curve where the amount halves in equal time steps, like your cold drink, is called exponential decay. If the activity is 800 Bq at 0 hours, what is it after 2 hours?

Yes, 400 Bq is right, because it's half of 800 after one half-life. A decay graph plots activity on the y-axis against time on the x-axis, and you read the half-life from it. The activity at 0 hours is 800 Bq; at 4 hours, what would the activity be?

Yes, 200 Bq is right, because it's half of 400 after another half-life. This marker has to give out radiation that gets out through the body to reach the camera. Which type of radiation do you think gets all the way out?

turns.reply: Sorry, that was a lot. A tracer is a radioactive marker the patient swallows, and a camera outside the body has to detect it, so its radiation must get right out through the body. Gamma rays pass through the body to the camera. So which radiation does the tracer give out: gamma?

Radiotherapy is a different use: a tumour is a lump of cancer cells, and a focused beam of gamma rays can be aimed at it, or a radioactive source can be placed inside the body close to it. What do you think the radiation does to the cancer cells?

Radiotherapy just means using radiation as a treatment. A tumour is a lump of cancer cells, and radiotherapy aims radiation at it to destroy it, a bit like how heat kills germs. If a doctor wants to wipe out a tumour, why would they aim the beam right at the tumour and not at the whole body?
Lots of people find this part hard, so that's fine. Do you want me to just tell you the rest of it?

Okay, have a go. Radiotherapy uses radiation to kill the cancer cells in a tumour, and the beam is aimed only at the tumour, not the whole body. Why do you think the doctor wants to avoid hitting the rest of the body?

turns.student: cos it would kill the normal cells too?
turns.reply: Yes, normal cells would be killed too, which is why the beam is aimed only at the tumour. Being exposed to radiation, like standing near a radioactive rock, is called irradiation, and you don't become radioactive from it. What do you think would happen to the rock's radiation if you walked away?
recap: A tracer is a radioactive marker swallowed so a camera can follow it.
Tracers give out gamma rays, which pass right through the body.
Radiotherapy uses radiation to kill the cancer cells in a tumour.
Aim the beam only at the tumour, so normal cells aren't killed too.

turns.reply: Irradiation just means being exposed to radiation, like getting sunlight on your skin, and when the sun goes away you're no longer getting any. Standing near a radioactive rock works the same way: it sends radiation at you, but it doesn't make you radioactive. If you walked away from the rock, what would happen to the radiation reaching you?
Sorry, that was a lot. If you walked away, the radiation reaching you would stop. If radioactive dust sticks to your skin, what happens when you walk away?

Yes, it stays on you, and that's contamination. Scientists who study how radiation affects people publish their results so other scientists can check them before they're accepted. That's called peer review. Why might checking someone else's findings be useful?

Peer review means other scientists check someone's published findings before they're accepted. It's like a friend marking your homework to spot mistakes. Why might it help to have other scientists check a result?
This one takes a bit of getting used to. Do you want me to just tell you the rest of this one?

Contamination means radioactive material sits on or in you, so it keeps irradiating you even when you move away. Radiation is dangerous because it damages DNA, and that can cause cancer. Protection means distance, shielding and short exposure time.

That's the end of this lesson. You answered questions on "Reading and drawing decay graphs" and "Uses of nuclear radiation", answered some on "What half-life means" and "Contamination, irradiation and radiation dangers", and I told you the rest. Come back any time.
